FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.84  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.78  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.solve()` can return an allocation that violates HARD feasibility constraints while presenting it as a normal successful result. The method computes `feasible, violations = self._check_feasibility(...)`, emits only a warning on failure, then still computes cost/balance and returns the invalid `Allocation`. In this area, F1/F2/F3 are explicitly documented as HARD constraints, so returning an infeasible plan as if it were a valid solution breaks the contract between optimization and orchestration. This is distinct from the already-found greedy fallback issues: even if the bad matrix arises for any reason, `solve()` normalizes it into a regular success path rather than surfacing infeasibility structurally. Downstream code can therefore dispatch an allocation known to violate capacity or role constraints.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Change the API so infeasibility is explicit and non-silent. Options: (1) raise a dedicated `AllocationInfeasibleError` containing violations; or (2) return `(alloc, cost, balanced, feasible, violations)` and require callers to branch on `feasible` before dispatch. If degraded operation is intentionally allowed, represent it with a separate result type/status enum rather than a warning.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.76  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.67  
DESCRIPTION: `_balanced()` and `_objective()` treat zero-capacity models as having load fraction `0.0` via `np.where(limits > 0, loads / limits, 0.0)`. If a model has `L == 0` and receives no load, it contributes an apparently perfect utilization of 0; if it receives load, feasibility catches overload, but the objective/balance metrics still mischaracterize the load profile. This distorts the balancing term and bottleneck term by making unusable models appear harmlessly idle rather than undefined/unavailable. In edge cases with one or more `L == 0` models, the solver can report `balanced=True` even though the pool contains non-serviceable participants that should likely be excluded from balance calculations or treated as saturated/unavailable.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate `L > 0` for dispatchable models at construction/config time, or exclude `L == 0` models from allocation and balance/objective calculations. If such models must remain in the pool, define their fraction as `inf` when loaded and omit them from balance variance when unloaded, with explicit policy documentation.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.72  
FLAW_CLASS: 4  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.63  
DESCRIPTION: `validate_homogeneous()` does not validate the stated reduction property “equal distribution optimal”; it only checks the boolean `balanced` predicate on one handcrafted instance. That means the validator can pass even when the produced allocation is not equal, not optimal, and only happens to have variance below `epsilon_bal`. This weakens the self-checking claims in the module, especially because the docstring presents these validators as reduction-property validations. The function name and docstring overstate what is actually tested.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Either rename the method to reflect what it actually checks (`validate_homogeneous_balancing_smoke_test`) or strengthen it to verify the claimed property: inspect per-model loads, assert near-equal distribution under homogeneous costs/limits, and compare objective value against plausible alternative allocations.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.69  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.__init__()` accepts arbitrary `role_map` contents without validating that every model has exactly one explicit role and that no extraneous IDs are present. Later, `_admissibility_mask()` uses `self.role_map.get(model.model_id, Role.PAR)`, silently defaulting any missing model to `PAR`. This can mask upstream role-assignment errors and broaden permissions unexpectedly: a model omitted from `role_map` becomes admissible for standard tasks rather than causing an immediate configuration failure. That is especially risky because role admissibility is a HARD constraint in this area.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate in `__init__` that `set(role_map.keys()) == {m.model_id for m in models}` and reject missing or unknown IDs. Remove the permissive `Role.PAR` default in `_admissibility_mask()` and use direct lookup after validation.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.61  
FLAW_CLASS: 8  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.49  
DESCRIPTION: The `solve()` return value and examples imply the returned `cost` is the cost of a valid allocation, but in practice it may be the score of an infeasible matrix because `_objective()` is evaluated regardless of feasibility. This makes the reported scalar hard to interpret: it mixes optimization score with known-invalid plans and can mislead downstream comparisons (“lower cost” may simply mean “more illegal”). The docstring does not disclose this semantic caveat.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Only compute/report objective for feasible allocations, or return it under a distinct field such as `raw_score` together with explicit feasibility metadata. Update docstrings/examples to state whether cost is defined for infeasible plans.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.54  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.44  
DESCRIPTION: `validate_k1()` can return `True` even when the single-model instance is infeasible by capacity. It only checks that each task is assigned to the sole model, not that the allocation satisfies the documented reduction condition `sum b_j <= L1`. Because `solve()` may force-assign over capacity and merely warn, this validator can falsely “validate” the K=1 reduction on overloaded examples if the fixture or future edits exceed capacity. The current fixture happens to fit, but the implementation does not actually test the stated property.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Extend `validate_k1()` to also check total demand `<= L`, verify feasibility explicitly, and fail if `_check_feasibility()` reports any violation.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F007  
SEVERITY: 0.47  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.40  
DESCRIPTION: `dispatch_check()` and `feasibility_probability()` are instance methods on `LoadBalancer` but do not depend on any allocation state except `self.config.feasibility_threshold` in `dispatch_check()`. This couples a per-model probabilistic capacity check to the load-balancing object even though it is semantically a model/dispatch policy utility. The result is an awkward API boundary: callers need a balancer instance to ask a local probabilistic question unrelated to a computed allocation. This contributes to the already-documented disconnect between feasibility estimation and solving.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Move probabilistic feasibility into a separate utility/policy object or make `feasibility_probability` a `@staticmethod` and `dispatch_check` a lightweight policy helper. Then integrate it explicitly into solving/dispatch orchestration if it is meant to affect decisions.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_X001  
SEVERITY: 0.58  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.55  
DESCRIPTION: [UNVERIFIED cross-component] The load balancer indexes models by `model_id` in `self._model_idx`, but no uniqueness validation is shown for `ModelSpec.model_id`. If duplicate model IDs are allowed upstream, `role_map`, `Allocation.model_ids`, and any caller using `get_assigned_tasks(model_id)` will become ambiguous or wrong because dictionary lookups collapse duplicates while the allocation matrix still has multiple columns. I cannot confirm from this area alone whether `ModelSpec` or `DynamicManager` enforces uniqueness globally.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Enforce unique `task_id` and `model_id` invariants at object construction boundaries (`LoadBalancer`, `Allocation`, or `ModelSpec` registry) and fail fast on duplicates.  
VERIFIED: FALSE

Definitive stance: the strongest new issues in Load Balancing are the acceptance of infeasible allocations as normal solver outputs, silent role-map defaulting, and validator methods that do not actually verify their claimed reduction properties.
